title: Read the whole number
subject: mind
native_material: price tags, odometers, the 2005 experiments and the 22-million-car auction study
hook_mechanism: the viewer is asked which price is bigger and feels the pull of the 2 before the answer
metaphors: the left digit as the price your brain actually pays attention to

pick.owner_words: "give me video of anything. free hand, do not ask me. choose any topic. 30 seconds" (the owner delegated the topic and the pick; historical-echo excluded as the last film's engine, reverse-autopsy as the one before)

concept.logline: Your eyes reach the left digit first, so $2.99 feels like two dollars and a car at 50,000 miles feels older than one at 49,999.
concept.central_question: Why does $2.99 feel so much cheaper than $3?
concept.claim: People anchor on the leftmost digit (Thomas and Morwitz 2005); the same bias moves used-car prices at every 10,000-mile mark (Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor 2012).

scenes.narration: Quick. Which costs more: two ninety-nine, or three dollars?
Three dollars. But your eyes read from the left.
scenes.graphic: Counter: $3.00 → $2.99 | one cent apart | the same price, read left to right

scenes.narration: They land on the two first, and your brain files the price as about two.
Experiments in 2005 gave it a name: the left-digit effect.
scenes.graphic: BigNumber: 2005 | magnifying glass | Thomas and Morwitz experiments | badge: verified

scenes.narration: It moves car prices too: over twenty-two million wholesale sales.
Roll the odometer one mile past a ten-thousand mark...
scenes.graphic: Counter: 49,999 → 50,000 | miles | one mile, a new left digit

scenes.narration: and the car sold for about a hundred and fifty to two hundred dollars less.
scenes.graphic: BigNumber: $200 | car | about $150 to $200 less (Lacetera, Pope, Sydnor, 2012) | badge: verified

scenes.narration: Next time, read the whole number.
